Su-35S: 155+ {{Cite web|url=https://function.mil.ru/news_page/country/more.htm?id=12398526@egNews|title=Партия новых самолетов Су-35с поступила в Липецкий авиацентр ВКС : Министерство обороны Российской Федерации|access-date=17 March 2023}} {{cite web | title=Russia Defies Sanctions as UAC Delivers Seventh Su-35S Batch to VKS in Record-Breaking 2025 Fighter Production Surge | date=25 December 2025 | url=https://defencesecurityasia.com/en/russia-su-35s-seventh-batch-delivery-record-2025-fighter-production/ }} | developed_from = [[Sukhoi Su-27]] | variants = [[Sukhoi Su-37]] | developed_into = }} The '''Sukhoi Su-35''' ({{langx|ru|link=no|Сухой Су}}-35; [[NATO reporting name]]: '''Flanker-E/M''', occasionally nicknamed "'''Super Flanker'''") is the designation for two improved derivatives of the Russian [[Sukhoi Su-27|Su-27]] air superiority fighter. They are single-seat, [[twinjet|twin-engine]], [[supermaneuverability|supermaneuverable]], 4.5 generation [[air superiority fighter]]s, designed by the [[Sukhoi Design Bureau]] and built by [[Sukhoi]]. The type was originally developed by the [[Soviet Union]] from the Su-27 and was known as the '''Su-27M'''. It incorporated [[Canard (aeronautics)|canards]] and a multi-function radar giving it multi-role capabilities. The first prototype made its [[maiden flight]] in June 1988. Following the [[dissolution of the Soviet Union]], Sukhoi relabeled it '''Su-35''' in hopes of attracting export orders. Fourteen aircraft were produced and used for tests and demonstrations; one example had [[Thrust vectoring|thrust-vectoring]] engines and was in turn redesignated the [[Sukhoi Su-37|Su-37]]. A sole Su-35UB two-seat trainer was also built in the late 1990s that resembled the [[Sukhoi Su-30|Su-30MK]] family. In 2003, Sukhoi embarked on a second "deep" modernization of the Su-27 to serve as an interim export aircraft awaiting the development of the [[Sukhoi PAK FA]] (Su-57) program. Also known as the Su-35, this version incorporates technology from the PAK FA program and has a redesigned cockpit and weapons-control system and features thrust-vectoring engines in place of the canards.{{cite news |last=Butowski|first=Piotr |title=Halfway to PAK FA: the latest addition to the Su-27 family seeks to bridge the gap to the fifth generation combat aircraft |url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-126558892.html |date=22 June 2004 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924122311/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-126558892.html|url-status=usurped|archive-date=24 September 2015|work=Interavia Business & Technology |publisher=Aerospace Media Publishing|access-date=19 April 2013 |via=[[HighBeam Research]]|url-access=subscription|oclc=71365085}} The type made its first flight in February 2008. Although it was designed for export, the [[Russian Air Force]] became the launch customer in 2009, with the production version designated Su-35S. China's [[People's Liberation Army Air Force]] has also placed orders. ==Design and development== ===Upgraded Su-27{{anchor|Su-27M/Su-35}}=== The first aircraft design to receive the Su-35 designation had its origins in the early 1980s, at a time when the [[Sukhoi Su-27|Su-27]] was being introduced into service with the [[Soviet Armed Forces]]. The definitive production version of the Su-27, which had the factory code of T-10S, started mass ("serial") production with the [[Komsomolsk-on-Amur Aircraft Production Association]] (KnAAPO) in 1983. The following year, this Su-27 version reached initial operational readiness with the [[Soviet Air Defence Forces]].{{Cite journal|last=Butowski|first=Piotr|date=1 November 1999|title=Dominance by design: the reign of Russia's 'Flankers' – PART ONE|journal=[[Jane's Intelligence Review]]|location=Coulsdon, UK|publisher=Jane's Information Group|volume=11|issue=11|issn=1350-6226}} Having begun work on an upgraded Su-27 variant in 1982,{{Sfn |Gordon| 2007| page =69}} the Sukhoi Design Bureau was instructed in December 1983 by the [[Soviet Council of Ministers]] to use the Su-27 as the basis for the development of the Su-27M (T-10M).{{sfn|Andrews|2003|page=39}} Nikolay Nikitin would lead the design effort throughout much of the project's existence, under the oversight of [[General Director]] [[Mikhail Simonov]], who had been the chief designer of the Su-27{{Sfn |Gordon| 2007| pages =58, 122}} along with [[Mikhail Pogosyan]].{{citation needed|date=July 2020}} [[File:Sukhoi Su-35 (Su-27M).png|thumb|upright|left|Planform view of the Su-27M]] While sharing broadly the [[blended wing body|blended wing-body]] design of the Su-27, the Su-27M is visibly distinguished from the basic version by the addition of [[canard (aeronautics)|canards]], which are small lifting surfaces, ahead of the wings. First tested in 1985 using an experimental aircraft, the canards, in complement with the reshaped wing [[leading-edge extension]], redirected the airflow in such a way so as to eliminate [[buffeting]] at high [[angle of attack|angles of attack]] and allowed the airframe to sustain 10-''g'' manoeuvres (as opposed to 9 ''g'' on the Su-27) without additional structural reinforcement.Fink 1993, p. 45. More importantly, when working with the [[Relaxed stability|relaxed-stability]] design and the accompanying [[fly-by-wire]] [[Aircraft flight control system|flight-control system]], the aerodynamic layout improved the aircraft's manoeuvrability and enabled it to briefly fly with its nose past the vertical while maintaining forward momentum. Because of this, theoretically, during combat the pilot could pitch the Su-27M up 120 degrees in under two seconds and fire missiles at the target.{{Sfn |Gordon| 2007| pages =122-123}} Other notable visible changes compared to the T-10S design included taller [[Vertical stabilizer|vertical tails]], provisions for [[Aerial refueling|in-flight refuelling]] and the use of two-wheel nose undercarriage to support the heavier airframe.Williams 2002, p. 119.{{Sfn |Gordon| 2007| pages =123,127}} Besides the increase in manoeuvrability, another feature that distinguished the Su-27M from the original design was the new [[Fire-control system|weapons-control system]]. The centrepiece of this system was the multi-function [[Bars radar|N011 Bars]] (literally "Leopard") [[phased array|phased-array]] radar with [[pulse-Doppler radar|pulse-Doppler]] tracking that allowed it to [[Look-down/shoot-down|detect targets below the horizon]]. First installed on the third prototype, the radar transformed the Su-27M from simply being an air-defence fighter into a multi-role aircraft capable of attacking ground targets.{{Sfn|Gordon|2007| page =124}} Compared to the [[Mech radar|N001 Myech]] ("Sword") radar of the Su-27, which could track 10 targets and only direct two missiles towards one target at a time, the new radar could track fifteen targets and direct missiles towards six of them simultaneously. The extra weight of the N011 radar at the front of the aircraft necessitated the addition of the canards; engineers would only later discover the aerodynamic advantages of these devices.{{sfn|Butowski|2004a|page= 38}}{{sfn|Gordon|2007|page=69}} In addition, an [[Phazotron N-012|N012]] self-defence radar was housed in the rearward-projecting tail boom, making the aircraft the first in the world to have such a radar.{{Sfn|Gordon|2007| page =124}} Other changes to the aircraft included the use of uprated turbofan engines, as well as the increased use of lightweight [[Composite material|composites]] and [[aluminium-lithium alloy]]s in the aircraft's structure.{{sfn|Gordon|2007|page=123}} ===Testing and demonstration=== In 1987, Sukhoi started converting the first prototype (designated {{Nowrap|T10M-1}}) from a T-10S airframe at its experimental plant in Moscow. Although it had canards, the first prototype, like several subsequent aircraft, lacked the many physical alterations of the new design.{{Sfn|Gordon|2007|pages =126, 127}} It made its first flight after conversion on 28 June 1988, piloted by Oleg Tsoi, followed by the second prototype in January 1989.{{Sfn|Gordon|2007| page =128}} Following the conversions of the two Su-27M prototypes, the actual production of the aircraft was transferred to the [[Russian Far East|country's Far East]] where it was carried out by KnAAPO. The third aircraft ({{Nowrap|T10M-3}}), which was the first new-built Su-27M and first to be constructed by KnAAPO, made its first flight in April 1992.{{Sfn|Gordon|2007| page =128}} By then, the Soviet Union [[Dissolution of the Soviet Union|had disintegrated]], and the ensuing economic crisis in Russia throughout the 1990s meant that the original plan to mass-produce the aircraft between 1996 and 2005 was abandoned, with the aircraft to serve as experimental test-beds to validate the canards, the flight-control system and thrust-vectoring technology. In total, two prototypes, nine flying pre-production and three production aircraft were constructed by 1995;{{sfn|Butowski|2004a|page= 38}}{{cite web|url=http://www.airwar.ru/enc/fighter/su35.html|title=Су-35|website=airwar.ru|access-date=23 February 2020}} the production aircraft were delivered in 1996 to the [[Russian Air Force]] for weapons testing.{{sfn|Gordon|2007|page=366}} [[File:Su-35 (12509727094).jpg|thumb|left|The ninth Su-27M in-flight]] By the time of the disintegration of the Soviet Union, Sukhoi had been demonstrating the Su-27M to senior defence and government officials. With its debut to a Western audience at the 1992 [[Farnborough Airshow]], the company redesignated the aircraft as Su-35.{{Sfn|Gordon|2007| pages =129-131}} The aircraft subsequently made flying demonstrations overseas in an effort to attract export orders, starting in November 1993 with [[Dubai Airshow|Dubai]], where [[Viktor Pugachev]] flew it in a mock aerial engagement with an Su-30MK in front of spectators.{{sfn|Fink|1993| p=44}}{{Sfn|Gordon|2007| pages =134-135}} The aircraft then flew in [[ILA Berlin Air Show|Berlin]] and [[Paris Air Show|Paris]], and would be a regular feature at Moscow's [[MAKS Air Show]].{{Sfn|Gordon|2007| pages =134-135}} The Russian government cleared the aircraft for export during Sukhoi's unsuccessful sales campaign in South Korea during the late 1990s and early 2000s;''Flight International'' 2001, p. 20. the company also marketed the aircraft to Brazil, China and the United Arab Emirates.{{sfn|Andrews|2003|page=58}} As the flight-test programme of the Su-27M proceeded, engineers discovered that the pilot failed to maintain active control of the aircraft during certain manoeuvres, such as the [[Pugachev's Cobra]]. The eleventh Su-27M ({{Nowrap|T10M-11}}) was therefore equipped with [[thrust-vectoring]] engine nozzles in 1995, and the resultant [[Sukhoi Su-37|Su-37]] [[Technology demonstration|technology demonstrator]] made its first flight on 2 April 1996.{{Sfn|Gordon|2007| pages =142, 144}}{{sfn|Velovich|1996|p=16}} It also tested the enhanced N011M radar, as did the twelfth developmental Su-27M.{{sfn|Andrews|2003|page=58}} The Su-37's ability to maintain a high angle of attack while flying at close to zero [[airspeed]] attracted considerable press attention.{{sfn|Novichkov|1996| p=52}} It later received different engines and updated fly-by-wire controls and cockpit systems for evaluation.{{sfn|Andrews|2003|page=58}} Apart from the single-seat design, a two-seat aircraft was also constructed. Working in cooperation with Sukhoi, KnAAPO's own engineers designed the Su-35UB so as to combine thrust-vectoring engines with features of the Su-27M. Modified from an [[Sukhoi Su-30MKK|Su-30MKK]] airframe, the aircraft made its first flight on 7 August 2000, and afterwards served as an avionics test-bed.{{Sfn|Gordon|2007| page =172-173}} While the original Su-27M never entered mass production due to a lack of funding,{{sfn|Barrie|1997| p=8}} Sukhoi refined the Su-27M's use of canards and the Su-37's thrust-vectoring technology and later applied them to the [[Su-30MKI]] two-seat fighter for the [[Indian Air Force]].{{sfn|Andrews|2003|page=47}} The tenth Su-27M (T10M-10) also served as a test-bed for the Saturn AL-41F1 engine that is intended for the [[Sukhoi Su-57]] (previously known under the acronym "PAK FA") jet fighter.{{Sfn|Gordon|2007|page =173}} ===Modernization=== [[File:Sukhoi Su-35S 07 RED PAS 2013 07.jpg|thumb|Thrust vectoring nozzle on a Sukhoi Su-35S]] With the need to update Russia's ageing fleet of [[Su-27]] aircraft, Sukhoi and KnAAPO in 2002 started integrating [[glass cockpit]]s and improved weapons-control systems (to accommodate a greater variety of weapons) to air force aircraft. The Su-27SM, as the modified aircraft is called, made its first flight in December 2002.{{sfn|Fiszer|2004|pages=52-53}} The success of this project led Sukhoi in December 2003 to proceed with a follow-up "deep" modernization programme. Known internally as T-10BM,{{sfn|Butowski|2004a|page= 38}} the programme was aimed at a more thorough redesign of the airframe to narrow the qualitative gap between Russian aircraft and foreign [[fourth-generation jet fighter|fourth-generation aircraft]]. The resultant design, also designated Su-35, would serve as an interim solution pending the introduction of the [[Post-PFI Soviet/Russian aircraft projects#PAK FA|PAK FA]] [[fifth-generation jet fighter|fifth-generation fighter]] (which eventually became the [[Sukhoi Su-57|Su-57]]), many features of which the aircraft would incorporate.{{sfn|Butowski|2004a|page= 38}}{{sfn|Fiszer|2004|page=53}}{{sfn|Butowski|2007|pages=34–35}} The aircraft was primarily aimed at the export market, being offered by KnAAPO as a single-seat alternative to the two-seat [[Sukhoi Su-30|Su-30MK]] variants built by [[Irkutsk Aviation Plant]] (IAP).{{cite web |last=Butowski |first=Piotr |url=https://www.key.aero/article/sukhoi-su-35-ultimate-flanker |title= Sukhoi Su-35 The Ultimate Flanker |work=Key Publishing |date=10 May 2021}}{{cite web |url=http://www.defenseindustrydaily.com/russias-su-35-mystery-fighter-no-more-04969/ |title=Russia's Su-35 Super-Flanker: Mystery Fighter No More |work=Defense Industry Daily |date=27 March 2013 |access-date=20 April 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130501070942/http://www.defenseindustrydaily.com/Russias-SU-35-Mystery-Fighter-No-More-04969/ |archive-date=1 May 2013}} In many aspects, the T-10BM design resembles the Su-27 more than the Su-27M. During tests of the thrust-vectoring engines and the Su-27M's aerodynamic layout, Sukhoi had concluded that the loss of manoeuvrability due to the removal of the canards – the addition of which imposed a weight penalty on the airframe – could be compensated for by the addition of thrust-vectoring nozzles.{{#tag:ref|"While the canard layout brought advantages in terms of improved manoeuvrability, it also added structural weight to the airframe. A conventional airframe coupled with thrust vector control, the source said, could now provide the same capability."Barrie 2003, p. 39:|group="N"}} Industry progress in the fields of avionics and radars has also reduced the weight and size of such components, which shifts the [[centre of gravity]] of an aircraft rearward.{{sfn|Butowski|2004a|page= 39}} Accordingly we saw SW, designers removed the canards (and the dorsal [[Air brake (aircraft)|air brake]]) found on the Su-27M; the size of the vertical tails, aft-cockpit hump and tail boom were also reduced.{{sfn|Butowski|2004a|page= 39}} With such changes, as well as the increased use of aluminium and [[titanium alloy]]s and composites, designers had reduced the empty weight of the aircraft, while maintaining a similar [[maximum take-off weight]] to the Su-27M.{{Cite web|first=Vladimir|last=Karnozov|url=https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/sukhoi-unveils-su-35-l-216386/|title=Sukhoi unveils 'supercruising' Su-35-1 multi-role fighter|date=4 September 2007|work=Flightglobal|access-date=22 July 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170808021053/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/sukhoi-unveils-su-35-l-216386/|archive-date=8 August 2017}}Kopp 2010, p. 9. [[File:MAKS Airshow 2013 (Ramenskoye Airport, Russia) (523-02).jpg|thumb|left|Su-35S cockpit layout: a [[head-up display]], two multi-function liquid crystal displays, and a control stick with [[HOTAS]] controls]] While the Su-27M design had the avionics to give the aircraft the nominal designation as a multi-role fighter, flight tests with the Russian Air Force revealed difficulties in deploying the aircraft's armament efficiently. According to ''[[Aviation Week & Space Technology]]'', air force pilots described weapons trials with the aircraft in [[Akhtubinsk (air base)|Akhtubinsk]] and [[Lipetsk (air base)|Lipetsk]] as a "negative experience", with a particular emphasis on the layout of the cockpit and its adverse impact on the workload of the single pilot. Designers, test pilots and avionics software specialists therefore worked together to redesign the cockpit and its attendant systems and improve the [[User interface|human-machine interface]]. The information management system of aircraft's avionics suite had been changed so that it now has two digital computers which process information from the flight- and weapons-control systems. The information is then displayed on two {{Convert|9|×|12|in|cm|abbr=on}} multi-function liquid crystal displays,{{cite web|url=http://www.sukhoi.org/eng/planes/military/Su-35/|title=Su-35|publisher=Sukhoi|access-date=25 April 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130502190948/http://sukhoi.org/eng/planes/military/Su-35/|archive-date=2 May 2013}} which replaced the smaller multi-function [[cathode-ray tube]] displays found on the Su-27M. The pilot can also view critical flight information on the [[head-up display]], and is equipped with [[HOTAS|Hands On Throttle-And-Stick]] (HOTAS) controls. The Su-35 employs the [[Irbis-E|N035 Irbis-E]] ("Snow Leopard") [[passive electronically scanned array]] (PESA) radar, which is a further development of the N011M radar that had been evaluated on Su-27M test-beds and constitutes the core of the Su-35's weapons-control system. It is capable of detecting an aerial target up to {{Convert|400|km|mi nmi|abbr=on}} away, and can track thirty airborne targets and engage eight of them simultaneously; in addition, the multi-function radar is capable of providing high-resolution images of the ground using [[Synthetic aperture radar|synthetic aperture mode]].{{sfn|Gordon|2007|page=175}} The aircraft is equipped with an OLS-35 optoelectronic targeting system ahead of the cockpit to provide other forms of tracking including [[infra-red search and track]]; other electro-optical systems include the OAR [[missile approach warning system]] and T-220 [[targeting pod]].{{sfn|Gordon|2007|page=175}} For defences against enemy tracking, the Su-35 is equipped with the [[Khibiny (electronic countermeasures system)|L175M Khibiny-M]] [[electronic countermeasure]] system,{{Cite web|url=http://www.defenceweb.co.za/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=15220|title=Sukhoi begins flight testing of Su-35S variant|date=6 May 2011|work=Defenceweb.co.za|access-date=30 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170830022756/http://www.defenceweb.co.za/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=15220|archive-date=30 August 2017}} while engineers have applied [[radar-absorbent material]]s to the engine inlets and front stages of the [[Jet engine compressors|engine compressor]] to halve the Su-35's frontal [[radar cross-section]] and minimize the detection range of enemy radars.Sweetman 2004, p. 26. The radar cross section of the Su-35 is reportedly 1 to 3 square meters.{{cite news |author=Alex Lockie |title=Here's who'd win in a dogfight between Russia's and the US's top fighter jets |url=https://www.businessinsider.com/su-35-vs-f-22-2016-9#stealth-6 |access-date=27 January 2024 |work=Business Insider |date=16 September 2016}} The N035 and Khibiny-M systems are integrated into the aircraft's Sh135 weapons control complex. The multi-role Su-35 can deploy air-to-air missiles of up to {{Convert|300|km|mi|adj=on}} range, and can carry the heavy [[P-800 Oniks|Oniks]] [[anti-ship missile|anti-ship]] [[cruise missile]], as well as a multitude of [[air-to-ground weaponry]].Butowski 2007, p. 36.{{sfn|Gordon|2007|pages=175-176}} {| class="toccolours" style="float: right; margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 2em; font-size: 100%; background:#c6dbf7; color:black; width:25em; max-width: 40%;" cellspacing="5" | style="text-align: left;" | "The classical air combat starts at high speed, but if you miss on the first shot—and the probability is there because there are maneuvers to avoid missiles—the combat will be more prolonged. After maneuvering, the aircraft will be at a lower speed, but both aircraft may be in a position where they cannot shoot. But supermaneuverability allows an aircraft to turn within three seconds and take another shot." |- | style="text-align: left;" | — Sergey Bogdan, Sukhoi chief test pilot |} The Su-35 is powered by a pair of [[Saturn AL-31#117S|Saturn AL-41F1S]] turbofan engines, formerly known as ''izdeliye'' (Product) 117S. A highly upgraded variant of the AL-31F, the AL-41F1S is closely related to the Su-57's [[Saturn AL-31#117|Saturn AL-41F1]] (''izdeliye'' 117), differing primarily in the engine control system.{{sfn|Butowski|2004a|pages= 39-40}}Butowski ''Air International'' October 2019, p. 37. The engines are equipped with thrust-vectoring nozzles, which have their rotational axes canted at an angle; the nozzles operate in one plane for pitch, but the canting allows the aircraft to produce both [[Flight dynamics|roll and yaw]] by vectoring each engine nozzle differently; this configuration was first implemented on the [[Sukhoi Su-30MKI|Su-30MKI]] and is also used on the Su-57.Sweetman 2013, p. 44. The Su-35's thrust-vectoring system and integrated flight- and propulsion-control systems allow the aircraft to attain 9-''g'' manoeuvres and "[[supermaneuverability]]", enabling it to perform [[Post stall|post-stall]] manoeuvres at low speeds. This differs from Western air combat doctrine, which emphasizes the maintenance of a fighter aircraft's [[kinetic energy]].{{Cite news|last=Bill|first=Sweetman|url=https://aviationweek.com/Article.aspx?id=/article-xml/AW_06_24_2013_p33-589854.xml&p=1|title=Sukhoi Test Pilot Explains 'Supermaneuverability'|date=24 June 2013|agency=[[Aviation Week & Space Technology]]|access-date=24 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140304215955/http://www.aviationweek.com/Article.aspx?id=%2Farticle-xml%2FAW_06_24_2013_p33-589854.xml&p=1|archive-date=4 March 2014|url-status=live}} The engine gives the Su-35 the limited ability to sustain [[supersonic speed]] above Mach 1.1 without the use of [[afterburner]]s, also known as "[[supercruise]]". ===Testing and production=== [[File:Sukhoi Su-35S (28333541172).jpg|thumb|A Russian Aerospace Forces Su-35S during a standard takeoff procedure]] Following the completion of design work, KnAAPO constructed the first prototype, which was finished in mid-2007. The prototype, Su-35-1, was then transferred to the [[Gromov Flight Research Institute]] at [[Zhukovsky International Airport|Zhukovsky Airfield]], in preparation for its maiden flight.{{sfn|Fomin|2008|page=28}}{{cite news|last=Usov|first=Pavel|url=http://www.kommersant.ru/doc/743121|script-title=ru:На КнААПО поступят двигатели для Су-35|newspaper=Kommersant|language=ru|date=16 February 2007|access-date=20 April 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130823234739/http://www.kommersant.ru/doc/743121|archive-date=23 August 2013|url-status=dead}} On 19 February 2008, Sergey Bogdan took the aircraft aloft for its 55-minute first flight from Zhukovsky.{{sfn|Fomin|2008|page=28}}{{cite news|url=http://www.kommersant.ru/doc/837808|script-title=ru:Начались испытания новой "сушки"|language=ru|newspaper=Kommersant|date=19 December 2007|access-date=20 April 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029195851/http://www.kommersant.ru/doc/837808|archive-date=29 October 2013|url-status=dead}} Bogdan later piloted the second prototype on its maiden flight on 2 October from KnAAPO's [[Dzyomgi Airport]].{{cite press release|url=http://www.sukhoi.org/news/smi/arch/index.php?id=1963|script-title=ru:Начались испытания второго летного образца новейшего Су-35|publisher=Sukhoi|language=ru|date=3 October 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130824055911/http://www.sukhoi.org/news/smi/arch/index.php?id=1963|archive-date=24 August 2013|url-status=dead}} The flight-test programme was expected to involve three flying prototypes, but on 26 April 2009, a day before its scheduled maiden flight, the fourth Su-35 (there's a static test aircraft) crashed during a taxi run at Dzyomgi Airport. The aircraft struck a barrier at the end of the runway and was destroyed by fire; the pilot ejected and sustained burn injuries.{{cite news|last=Nechayev |first=Gennady However, the low number of purchases also signified that the deal was symbolic in nature, as the two countries are still competing over influence in Central Asia, according to Moritz Rudolf of [[Mercator Institute for China Studies]]. The first two prototypes had a new forward fuselage, canards and updated fly-by-wire flight-control systems. Like three of KNAAPO's nine flying pre-production aircraft (T10M-5, T10M-6 and T10M-7), they were converted from Su-27 airframes.{{sfn|Andrews|2003|page=57}}{{sfn|Gordon|2007|page=129}} The third aircraft (T10M-3) was the first of seven pre-production aircraft to have the taller vertical tails, two-wheel nose undercarriage and in-flight refuel capability.{{Sfn|Gordon|2007| page =128}} The Su-27M was powered by AL-31FM turbofan engines.{{sfn|Gordon|2007|page=123}} Two prototypes, nine pre-production and three production aircraft were constructed by 1995;{{sfn|Butowski|2004a|page= 38}} two static-test aircraft was also constructed (T10M-0 and T10M-4).{{Sfn |Gordon| 2007| pages =129,591}} The aircraft did not enter mass production. [[File:Sukhoi Su-37 at Farnborough 1996 airshow.jpg|thumb|Sukhoi Su-37 at [[Farnborough Airshow|Farnborough 1996 airshow]]]] ;[[Sukhoi Su-37|Su-37]]: Technology demonstrator, converted from the eleventh developmental Su-27M (T10M-11). The Su-37 featured a digital fly-by-wire flight-control system, a [[glass cockpit]], the N011M radar, and AL-31FP engines with thrust-vectoring nozzles.{{Sfn |Gordon| 2007| pages =151,154,158}} The aircraft was later fitted with standard-production AL-31F engines, and had its flight-control system and cockpit systems revised.{{Sfn |Gordon| 2007| pages =170,171}} [[File:Su-35UB.jpeg|thumb|The sole two-seat Su-35UB in 2001]] ;Su-35UB: Two-seat trainer designed and built by KnAAPO. The single aircraft (T-10UBM-1) featured the canards and taller vertical tails of the Su-27M and a forward fuselage similar to the Su-30MKK. The Su-35UB also shared the avionics suite of the Su-30MKK, although it had a different fly-by-wire flight-control system to accommodate the canards.{{sfn|Andrews|2003|page=59}} The aircraft was powered by AL-31FP engines with thrust-vectoring nozzles.{{Sfn |Gordon| 2007| page =172}} Although a training aircraft, the Su-35UB was designed to be fully combat-capable.{{sfn|Andrews|2003|page=59}} ;Su-35BM: Single-seat fighter that is a major redesign of the original Su-27. The type features significant modifications to the airframe, including the removal of canards and dorsal air brake as found on the Su-27M. It features the updated N035 Irbis-E radar and a redesigned cockpit. The aircraft is powered by thrust-vectoring AL-41F1S turbofan engines that are capable of supercruise. Also known as T-10BM (''Bolshaya Modernizatsiya'', "Major Modernization"), Su-35BM is not the actual designation used by Sukhoi, who markets the aircraft as "Su-35".{{cite web |last=Trimble |first=Stephen |url=http://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/russia-signs-25-billion-deal-for-64-sukhoi-fighters-331265/ |title=Russia signs $2.5 billion deal for 64 Sukhoi fighters |work=Flightglobal|date=20 August 2009 |access-date=18 July 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130824023307/http://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/russia-signs-25-billion-deal-for-64-sukhoi-fighters-331265/|archive-date=24 August 2013}} [[File:FighterAircraftExercise2020-01.jpg|thumb|A combat-ready Su-35S equipped with pairs of [[R-73 (missile)|R-73]], [[R-27 (air-to-air missile)|R-27]] and [[R-77]] [[air-to-air missile]]s in an exercise.]] ;Su-35S: Su-35S is the production designator for the T-10BM design for the Russian Aerospace Forces. According to ''Aviation Week & Space Technology'', "S" stands for ''Stroyevoy'' ("Combatant").{{sfn|Pyadushkin|Perrett|2014|page=19}} NATO reporting name Flanker-M.{{Cite web |date=2023-06-26 |title=Rostec State Corporation Delivers New Sukhoi Su-35S Fighter Jets to Russian Air Forces |url=https://militaryleak.com/2023/06/26/rostec-state-corporation-delivers-new-sukhoi-su-35s-fighter-jets-to-russian-air-forces/?amp=1 |access-date=2023-07-06 |website=MilitaryLeak |language=en-US}} The Flanker M is the latest version of the Sukhoi Su-35, known internally as the Su-35BM (bolshaya modernizatsiya – big modernization), and is an advanced capability multirole air superiority fighter developed from the Su-27. The aircraft has high manoeuvrability (+9g) with a high angle of attack, and is equipped with high-capability weapon systems that contribute to the new aircraft’s exceptional dogfighting capability. The Russian Air Force ordered 48 Sukhoi Su-35S fighters in August 2009 with deliveries scheduled to run until 2015. Sukhoi began producing the components required for assembly of the aircraft in November 2009. An information management system integrated with onboard subsystems and a new phased array radar system with long-range aerial target detection have been installed in the aircraft. The first Su-35S aircraft was handed over to the 929th State Flight Test Centre (GLITS) for flight tests in August 2011. The Russian Ministry of Defence received six Su-35S production aircraft from Sukhoi in December 2012. In 2015, China ordered 24 Su-35S aircraft for China’s People’s Liberation Army Air Force.{{Cite journal |date=2020-01-01 |title=Chapter Five: Russia and Eurasia |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/04597222.2020.1707966 |journal=The Military Balance |language=en |volume=120 |issue=1 |pages=166–219 |doi=10.1080/04597222.2020.1707966 |s2cid=219627993 |issn=0459-7222|url-access=subscription }} ;Su-35SM: Su-35SM is an upgrade to the Su-35S, designed for the [[Russian Aerospace Forces]]. This variant aims to enhance air superiority and electronic warfare capabilities. Notable upgrades include an [[active electronically scanned array]] (AESA) radar [[N036 Byelka]], similar to that used in the [[Su-57]], which will replace the [[Irbis-E]] radar, boosting detection range and resistance to countermeasures. The aircraft will also feature the “Himalaya” electronic warfare suite, offering advanced protection against radar-guided threats. New secure communications and data-link systems are included for better network-centric operations, along with a laser-based DIRCM system to counter infrared missiles. The airframe may use materials to lower radar visibility and be optimized for next-generation munitions like the [[R-37 (missile)|R-37M]] and [[R-77#Variants|R-77M]] missiles.{{Cite web |date=2023-01-13 |title=The Su-35SM will use an AESA radar and a Himalayan EW system|url=https://www.airspace-review.com/2023/01/13/su-35sm-akan-menggunakan-radar-aesa-dan-sistem-ew-himalaya/ }} ==Operators== [[File:Su-35 Operators.png|thumb|300px|Su-35 Operators]] ; {{Flagu|Algeria}} * [[Algerian Air Force]] - Out of the 25 that were produced for Egypt, nine are no longer visible on current satellite images.
